summary.text: Cosine-moment formulas for the central binomial and generalized trinomial coefficients convert the series into a triple integral, where summing a differentiated geometric series and evaluating one integral reduce it to a double integral. An explicit two-variable differential identity evaluates that integral by deforming the inner contour between radii \(1/2\) and \(1/6\); the sole crossed simple pole at \(w=-1/4\), occurring when \(\cos\beta=-7/25\), has residues \(\pm(385/2)i\), giving the required constant after normalization.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 T_k(b,c)=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}
 {k\choose j}{k-j\choose j}b^{k-2j}c^j.
\]
This is indeed the coefficient of \(x^k\) in \((x^2+bx+c)^k\): to obtain degree \(k\), one must choose \(j\) copies of \(x^2\), \(j\) copies of \(c\), and \(k-2j\) copies of \(bx\). We prove
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{4290k+367}{3136^k}{2k\choose k}
 T_k(14,1)T_k(17,16)=\frac{5390}{\pi}.
\]
The proof has two parts. First we evaluate a certain double integral by a contour argument. Then we expand that integral and identify its terms with the series above.

## 1. The real double integral

For real \(\beta,\gamma\), put
\[
 p(\beta,\gamma)=
 \frac{(14+2\cos\beta)(17+8\cos\gamma)}{784}
\]
and
\[
 F(\beta,\gamma)=
 \frac{367+1778p(\beta,\gamma)}{(\sqrt{1-p(\beta,\gamma)})^3}.
\]
Since \(-1\leq\cos\theta\leq1\),
\[
 0\leq p(\beta,\gamma)\leq \frac{16\cdot25}{784}
 =\frac{400}{784}<1.
\]
In particular all square roots in this definition are positive real square roots. The central analytic assertion is
\[
 \int_0^\pi\int_0^\pi F(\beta,\gamma)\,d\gamma\,d\beta
 =5390\pi. \tag{1}
\]
We now prove (1).

### 1.1. A rational differential certificate

For nonzero complex variables \(y,w\), define
\[
 \phi_2(y)=y+14+y^{-1},\qquad
 \phi_3(w)=4w+17+4w^{-1},
\]
\[
 Q(y,w)=\frac{\phi_2(y)\phi_3(w)}{784},
 \qquad S(y,w)=\sqrt{1-Q(y,w)},
 \qquad Z(y,w)=28ywS(y,w).
\]
Here the square root is the principal complex square root. On every region used below, \(1-Q\) has positive real part, so this branch is single-valued and holomorphic.

Set
\[
 \mathcal G(y,w)=-\frac{1778}{Z(y,w)}
 +\frac{1681680(yw)^2}{Z(y,w)^3}. \tag{2}
\]
We will use explicit polynomials \(B,P,D\). If a row \((a_0,\ldots,a_m)\) denotes \(a_0+a_1w+\cdots+a_mw^m\), then \(B(y,w)=\sum_r B_r(w)y^r\), where the rows \(B_0,\ldots,B_{13}\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
0&(0)\\
1&(0,-69300,-522900,2916900,-522900,-69300)\\
2&(-3889536,-34906424,199043656,-122477992,199043656,-34906424,-3889536)\\
3&(-457755648,2540755728,-3782286704,10161583152,-3782286704,2540755728,-457755648)\\
4&(-6288105600,34561871512,-2457433832,-25902367288,-2457433832,34561871512,-6288105600)\\
5&(-6833670144,-215802719748,2349513373340,-6422620273356,2349513373340,-215802719748,-6833670144)\\
6&(34382127360,-1576148827568,17036763527504,-56716109303056,17036763527504,-1576148827568,34382127360)\\
7&(0)\\
8&(-34382127360,1576148827568,-17036763527504,56716109303056,-17036763527504,1576148827568,-34382127360)\\
9&(6833670144,215802719748,-2349513373340,6422620273356,-2349513373340,215802719748,6833670144)\\
10&(6288105600,-34561871512,2457433832,25902367288,2457433832,-34561871512,6288105600)\\
11&(457755648,-2540755728,3782286704,-10161583152,3782286704,-2540755728,457755648)\\
12&(3889536,34906424,-199043656,122477992,-199043656,34906424,3889536)\\
13&(0,69300,522900,-2916900,522900,69300).
\end{array}
\]
Likewise \(P(y,w)=\sum_{r=0}^{12}P_r(w)y^r\), with
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
0&(0,0,69300,294525,0,-294525,-69300)\\
1&(0,3889536,22492400,-12324508,0,12324508,-22492400,-3889536)\\
2&(0,389184768,-351966552,611175866,0,-611175866,351966552,-389184768)\\
3&(0,4609670016,-4938186960,-16992372012,0,16992372012,4938186960,-4609670016)\\
4&(0,-55190037504,227961000204,-909895465549,0,909895465549,-227961000204,55190037504)\\
5&(0,26383166208,-944072254496,-744960434232,0,744960434232,944072254496,-26383166208)\\
6&(0,47608253952,-6133564617936,63953076732972,0,-63953076732972,6133564617936,-47608253952)\\
7&(0,26383166208,-944072254496,-744960434232,0,744960434232,944072254496,-26383166208)\\
8&(0,-55190037504,227961000204,-909895465549,0,909895465549,-227961000204,55190037504)\\
9&(0,4609670016,-4938186960,-16992372012,0,16992372012,4938186960,-4609670016)\\
10&(0,389184768,-351966552,611175866,0,-611175866,351966552,-389184768)\\
11&(0,3889536,22492400,-12324508,0,12324508,-22492400,-3889536)\\
12&(0,0,69300,294525,0,-294525,-69300).
\end{array}
\]
Finally let
\[
 D=D_{0a}D_{0b}D_1D_2, \tag{3}
\]
where
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_{0a}&=y^2+48yw-2y+1,\\
D_{0b}&=y^2w-2yw+48y+w,\\
D_1&=(y-1)^2(w^2+1)-2(y^2+6y+1)w,\\
D_2&=4096y(y^4+16y^3+30y^2+16y+1)(w^2+1)\\
&\quad +(225y^6-3398y^5-197329y^4-1696148y^3
 -197329y^2-3398y+225)w.
\end{aligned}
\]
Define
\[
 \widehat B=\frac{B}{DZ},\qquad A=\frac{P}{DZ}. \tag{4}
\]
The certificate is the differential identity
\[
 \frac{\partial\widehat B}{\partial y}
 -\frac{\partial A}{\partial w}=\mathcal G. \tag{5}
\]
We record how (5) is checked, so that the large displayed certificate is fully reproducible. Squaring the definition of \(Z\) gives
\[
 Z^2=784y^2w^2-yw(y^2+14y+1)(4w^2+17w+4). \tag{6}
\]
Differentiate (6), so that \(ZZ_y=\tfrac12(Z^2)_y\) and
\(ZZ_w=\tfrac12(Z^2)_w\). Apply the quotient rule to (4), put the two derivatives over the common denominator \(D^2Z^3\), and substitute (6) and its two derivatives. After multiplication by \(D^2Z^3\), (5) becomes a polynomial identity in \(y,w\). Expanding the rows in the two tables and the four factors in (3), the coefficients on the two sides agree term by term; the remaining numerator is exactly
\[
 \left(-1778Z^2+1681680y^2w^2\right)D^2,
\]
which, divided by \(D^2Z^3\), is (2). Thus (5) follows by ordinary polynomial arithmetic.

### 1.2. Domains on which the certificate has no singularities

Put \(y=e^{i\beta}\) and \(c=\cos\beta\). Then
\[
 y+y^{-1}=2c.
\]
In terms of \(c\), the factors of \(D\) become
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_{0a}&=y(2c-2+48w),\\
D_{0b}&=y(w(2c-2)+48),\\
D_1&=y\big((2c-2)(w^2+1)-(4c+12)w\big),\\
D_2&=y^3\big(16384(c+1)(c+7)(w^2+1)-q(c)w\big),
\end{aligned} \tag{7}
\]
where
\[
 q(c)=-1800c^3+13592c^2+396008c+1689352. \tag{8}
\]
For \(-1\leq c\leq1\), the first two factors are nonzero whenever
\(1/6\leq |w|\leq1\). Indeed, if \(D_{0a}=0\), then
\(48|w|=|2-2c|\leq4\), contrary to \(|w|\geq1/6\). If
\(D_{0b}=0\), then \(48=|w||2c-2|\leq4\).

For \(|w|=1/2\), if \(D_1=0\), taking absolute values in (7) gives
\[
 (2-2c)|w^2+1|=(4c+12)/2.
\]
Here \(|w^2+1|\leq5/4\). These inequalities are incompatible when
\(c>-7/9\). Thus
\[
 D_1\ne0\quad\text{on }|w|=1/2\text{ if }c>-7/9. \tag{9}
\]
For \(|w|=1/6\), use \(|w^2+1|\geq1-|w|^2=35/36\). The analogous equality is incompatible when \(c<-1/47\), and hence
\[
 D_1\ne0\quad\text{on }|w|=1/6\text{ if }c<-1/47. \tag{10}
\]

It remains to control \(D_2\). On \([-1,1]\), direct rearrangement gives
\[
 q(c)\geq131072(c+1)(c+7)=8\cdot16384(c+1)(c+7), \tag{11}
\]
because the difference follows from
\[
 (1-c)(1800c^2+119280c+771848)\geq0.
\]
Also \(q(c)>0\) on this interval (for example, expanding it as a positive combination using \((c-1)^2,(c+1)^2,c^2\) proves this directly). Let
\(r=|w|\), \(P_0=16384(c+1)(c+7)\). If \(D_2=0\), then
\[
 q(c)r=P_0|w^2+1|\leq P_0(r^2+1).
\]
By (11), this implies \(8P_0r\leq P_0(r^2+1)\). But for
\(1/6\leq r\leq1\), one has \(8r-r^2-1>0\). Hence \(P_0=0\), after which the displayed equality would give \(q(c)r\leq0\), impossible. Therefore \(D_2\ne0\) throughout this annulus.

Combining these observations,
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
D(e^{i\beta},w)\ne0&\text{on }|w|=1/2\quad\text{if }\cos\beta>-7/9,\\
D(e^{i\beta},w)\ne0&\text{on }|w|=1/6\quad\text{if }\cos\beta<-1/47.
\end{array} \tag{12}
\]

We also need to know that the chosen square root is analytic. For
\(1/6\leq|w|\leq1\),
\[
 \Re\phi_3(w)=4\Re w+17+4\Re(w^{-1})\leq4+17+24=45.
\]
Because \(12\leq14+2c\leq16\), considering separately whether
\(\Re\phi_3(w)\leq0\) or is positive shows
\[
 \Re(1-Q(e^{i\beta},w))>0. \tag{13}
\]
Indeed in the positive case its product with \(14+2c\) is at most
\(45\cdot16<784\), and in the nonpositive case the assertion is immediate. Thus \(S,Z,\mathcal G\), and the certificate are analytic wherever (12) says that \(D\ne0\). Notice also that \(Z\ne0\) there.

### 1.3. Contour primitives

All circles below are positively oriented. Define
\[
 \Psi_\rho(\beta)=\oint_{|w|=\rho}\widehat B(e^{i\beta},w)\,dw,
\]
\[
 K_\rho(\beta)=i e^{i\beta}
 \oint_{|w|=\rho}\mathcal G(e^{i\beta},w)\,dw. \tag{14}
\]
By (13), for fixed \(\beta\), \(\mathcal G(e^{i\beta},w)\) is holomorphic in
\(1/6\leq|w|\leq1\). Cauchy's theorem on an annulus therefore gives
\[
 K_\rho(\beta)=K_1(\beta)\qquad(1/6\leq\rho\leq1). \tag{15}
\]

On any open interval of \(\beta\)'s on which \(D\) does not vanish on
\(|w|=\rho\), differentiation under the contour integral is legitimate. Since
\(d(e^{i\beta})/d\beta=i e^{i\beta}\), identity (5) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \Psi_\rho'(\beta)
 &=i e^{i\beta}\oint_{|w|=\rho}
 \frac{\partial\widehat B}{\partial y}(e^{i\beta},w)\,dw\\
 &=i e^{i\beta}\oint_{|w|=\rho}
 \left(\frac{\partial A}{\partial w}+\mathcal G\right)(e^{i\beta},w)\,dw
 =K_\rho(\beta),
\end{aligned} \tag{16}
\]
because the integral of the derivative \(A_w\) around a closed curve is zero. The continuity needed here follows from (12)–(13); on a compact subinterval all derivatives are uniformly bounded, which also justifies differentiation under the integral sign.

Let
\[
 \beta_*=\arccos(-7/25),\qquad 0<\beta_*<\pi.
\]
On \([-\beta_*,\beta_*]\), monotonicity and evenness of cosine give
\(\cos\beta\geq-7/25>-7/9\). Hence (12), (15), and (16), with
\(\rho=1/2\), yield
\[
 \int_{-\beta_*}^{\beta_*}K_1(\beta)\,d\beta
 =\Psi_{1/2}(\beta_*)-\Psi_{1/2}(-\beta_*). \tag{17}
\]
On \([\beta_*,2\pi-\beta_*]\), splitting at \(\pi\) and using the monotonicity of cosine on \([0,\pi]\), one gets
\(\cos\beta\leq-7/25<-1/47\). Therefore, using \(\rho=1/6\),
\[
 \int_{\beta_*}^{2\pi-\beta_*}K_1(\beta)\,d\beta
 =\Psi_{1/6}(-\beta_*)-\Psi_{1/6}(\beta_*), \tag{18}
\]
where periodicity has been used at the upper endpoint.

### 1.4. The residue jump

At either endpoint, \(c=-7/25\). In that case (7) factors further as
\[
 D_1=-\frac{64}{25}y(w+4)(w+1/4). \tag{19}
\]
Let
\[
 D_{\rm rest}=D_{0a}D_{0b}D_2

a nd
\[
 f_y(w)=\frac{B(y,w)}{-(64/25)y(w+4)D_{\rm rest}(y,w)Z(y,w)}.
\]
(The isolated line break above is only typographical: the definition is
\(D_{\rm rest}=D_{0a}D_{0b}D_2\).)
Then (19) says
\[
 \widehat B(y,w)=\frac{f_y(w)}{w+1/4}. \tag{20}
\]
The estimates already proved show that \(f_y\) is holomorphic on
\(1/6\leq|w|\leq1/2\). The sole pole of (20) in this annulus is therefore
\(w=-1/4\), and it is simple. The residue theorem gives
\[
 \Psi_{1/2}(\beta)-\Psi_{1/6}(\beta)
 =2\pi i\,f_{e^{i\beta}}(-1/4)
 \quad\text{when }\cos\beta=-7/25. \tag{21}
\]
Equivalently, one may subtract
\(f_y(-1/4)/(w+1/4)\); the remainder extends holomorphically across
\(-1/4\), its two circle integrals agree, the large circle encloses
\(-1/4\), and the small one does not.

We now evaluate the two residues. Since \(\phi_3(-1/4)=0\), one has
\(Q(y,-1/4)=0\), \(S(y,-1/4)=1\), and
\[
 Z(y,-1/4)=-7y. \tag{22}
\]
Thus
\[
 f_y(-1/4)=
 \frac{B(y,-1/4)}{(336/5)y^2D_{\rm rest}(y,-1/4)}. \tag{23}
\]
The two endpoint values are
\[
 y_+=e^{i\beta_*}=\frac{-7+24i}{25},\qquad
 y_-=e^{-i\beta_*}=\frac{-7-24i}{25},
\]
and both satisfy
\[
 25y^2+14y+25=0. \tag{24}
\]
For completeness, direct substitution of the displayed polynomial \(B\) and reduction by (24) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
B(y,-1/4)&=
 \frac{2295075749707475440369664}{3814697265625}\\
&\quad-
 \frac{398895279373821343594184704}{95367431640625}
 y,
\end{aligned} \tag{25}
\]
and expansion of the three factors in \(D_{\rm rest}\), followed by the same quadratic reduction, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
y^2D_{\rm rest}(y,-1/4)&=
 -\frac{1336582694359969824768}{3814697265625}\\
&\quad-
 \frac{13614104370181153226752}{95367431640625}y.
\end{aligned} \tag{26}
\]
Substituting \(y_+\) and \(y_-\) in (23), using (25)–(26), and simplifying real and imaginary parts yields
\[
 f_{y_+}(-1/4)=\frac{385}{2}i,
 \qquad
 f_{y_-}(-1/4)=-\frac{385}{2}i. \tag{27}
\]
These denominators are nonzero; this also follows from the previously established nonvanishing of \(D_{\rm rest}\) and \(Z\).

Adding (17) and (18), then using (21), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{-\beta_*}^{2\pi-\beta_*}K_1(\beta)\,d\beta
&=\big(\Psi_{1/2}(\beta_*)-\Psi_{1/6}(\beta_*)\big)\\
&\quad-\big(\Psi_{1/2}(-\beta_*)-\Psi_{1/6}(-\beta_*)\big)\\
&=2\pi i\left(\frac{385}{2}i-
 \left(-\frac{385}{2}i\right)\right)=-770\pi.
\end{aligned} \tag{28}
\]
The function \(K_1\) is \(2\pi\)-periodic, so shifting the interval in (28) gives
\[
 \int_0^{2\pi}K_1(\beta)\,d\beta=-770\pi. \tag{29}
\]

### 1.5. Return to the real integrand

On the unit torus, \(y=e^{i\beta}\), \(w=e^{i\gamma}\), we have
\[
 Q(y,w)=p(\beta,\gamma),\qquad
 S(y,w)=\sqrt{1-p(\beta,\gamma)}.
\]
Using \(Z=28ywS\), \(p=1-S^2\), and (2), direct simplification gives
\[
 F(\beta,\gamma)=28yw\,\mathcal G(y,w). \tag{30}
\]
Indeed the right side is
\(-1778/S+1681680/(28^2S^3)
=(-1778S^2+2145)/S^3=(367+1778p)/S^3\).

Let
\[
 I(\beta)=\int_0^{2\pi}F(\beta,\gamma)\,d\gamma.
\]
Since \(dw=iw\,d\gamma\), equations (14) and (30) imply
\[
 I(\beta)=-28K_1(\beta). \tag{31}
\]
Integrating (31) and using (29),
\[
 \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}F(\beta,\gamma)\,d\gamma\,d\beta
 =21560\pi. \tag{32}
\]
The function \(F\) is continuous, even, and \(2\pi\)-periodic in each variable, since it depends on each variable only through its cosine. For any continuous even \(2\pi\)-periodic function \(h\), a change of variable on \([-\pi,0]\) shows
\[
 \int_0^{2\pi}h(x)\,dx=2\int_0^\pi h(x)\,dx.
\]
Apply this first in \(\gamma\), then in \(\beta\). Equation (32) becomes
\[
 4\int_0^\pi\int_0^\pi F(\beta,\gamma)\,d\gamma\,d\beta
 =21560\pi,
\]
which proves (1).

## 2. Conversion of the integral to the series

We now express (1) as the desired series. We first record three elementary integral formulas.

### 2.1. Cosine moments and coefficient integrals

The standard reduction formula for powers of cosine gives
\[
 \int_0^\pi\cos^{2j}\theta\,d\theta
 =\pi\frac{{2j\choose j}}{4^j},
 \qquad
 \int_0^\pi\cos^{2j+1}\theta\,d\theta=0. \tag{33}
\]
For example, the odd formula follows by the substitution
\(\theta\mapsto\pi-\theta\), while integration by parts gives the recurrence for the even moments; induction then gives the central-binomial expression.

Expanding \((b+2m\cos\theta)^k\), deleting the odd cosine powers by (33), and using
\[
 {k\choose 2j}{2j\choose j}={k\choose j}{k-j\choose j},

after cancellation of \(4^j\), yields
\[
 \frac1\pi\int_0^\pi(b+2m\cos\theta)^k\,d\theta
 =T_k(b,m^2). \tag{34}
\]
In particular,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^\pi(14+2\cos\beta)^k\,d\beta&=\pi T_k(14,1),\\
\int_0^\pi(17+8\cos\gamma)^k\,d\gamma&=\pi T_k(17,16).
\end{aligned} \tag{35}
\]
A second consequence of (33), using
\(2+2\cos\alpha=4\cos^2(\alpha/2)\), is
\[
 {2k\choose k}= rac1\pi\int_0^\pi(2+2\cos\alpha)^k\,d\alpha. \tag{36}
\]

### 2.2. An auxiliary one-dimensional integral

For \(0\leq p<1\), set
\[
 X(p,\alpha)=\frac{p(1+\cos\alpha)}2,
 \qquad
 f(p,\alpha)=\frac{367+3923X(p,\alpha)}{(1-X(p,\alpha))^2}.
\]
The geometric-series identity and its derivative give, for \(0\leq X<1\),
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^\infty(4290k+367)X^k
 =\frac{367+3923X}{(1-X)^2}. \tag{37}
\]
We also need the closed form
\[
 \int_0^\pi f(p,\alpha)\,d\alpha
 =\pi\frac{367+1778p}{(\sqrt{1-p})^3}. \tag{38}
\]
Here is a direct antiderivative verification. Put
\[
 A=1-p/2,\quad B=p/2,\quad D=\sqrt{1-p}.
\]
Then \(D^2=A^2-B^2\), \(0\leq B<A\), and differentiation shows
\[
 \frac d{d\alpha}\left[
 \alpha+2\arctan\frac{B\sin\alpha}{A-B\cos\alpha+D}
 \right]=\frac D{A-B\cos\alpha}, \tag{39}
\]
while
\[
 \frac d{d\alpha}\left[
 \frac{B\sin\alpha}{A-B\cos\alpha}
 \right]=\frac{AB\cos\alpha-B^2}{(A-B\cos\alpha)^2}. \tag{40}
\]
Consequently an antiderivative of \(f(p,\alpha)\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left(-3923+\frac{4290A}{1-p}\right)
 \frac1D\left(
 \alpha+2\arctan\frac{B\sin\alpha}{A-B\cos\alpha+D}
 \right)\\
&\qquad+\frac{4290}{1-p}
 \frac{B\sin\alpha}{A-B\cos\alpha}.
\end{aligned} \tag{41}
\]
This follows by combining (39) and (40) over a common denominator. At
\(\alpha=0,\pi\), the sine and arctangent terms vanish, so evaluation of (41), followed by \(D^2=1-p\), gives exactly (38).

Combining (38) with the definition of \(F\), we obtain
\[
 F(\beta,\gamma)=\frac1\pi
 \int_0^\pi f(p(\beta,\gamma),\alpha)\,d\alpha. \tag{42}
\]

### 2.3. Expansion and justified interchange

Let
\[
 r=\frac{400}{784}<1.
\]
For all three angles under consideration,
\(0\leq p(\beta,\gamma)\leq r\), and
\[
 0\leq X(p(\beta,\gamma),\alpha)\leq p(\beta,\gamma)\leq r.
\]
Thus the summands in (37) are bounded uniformly by
\[
 (4290k+367)r^k.
\]
This majorant is summable, being a linear combination of a geometric series and its derivative. Hence the Weierstrass test and dominated convergence permit termwise integration successively in \(\alpha,\gamma,\beta\).

For fixed \(p\), (36) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^\pi(4290k+367)X(p,\alpha)^k\,d\alpha
&=\pi(4290k+367){2k\choose k}\left(\frac p4\right)^k. \tag{43}
\end{aligned}
\]
Substitute
\[
 p=p(\beta,\gamma)
 =\frac{(14+2\cos\beta)(17+8\cos\gamma)}{784}.
\]
Because \(4\cdot784=3136\), integrating (43) in \(\gamma\) and using the second formula in (35) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\int_0^\pi\int_0^\pi
 (4290k+367)X(p(\beta,\gamma),\alpha)^k
 \,d\alpha\,d\gamma\\
&\quad=\pi^2(4290k+367){2k\choose k}
 \left(\frac{14+2\cos\beta}{3136}\right)^kT_k(17,16).
\end{aligned} \tag{44}
\]
A final integration in \(\beta\), using the first formula in (35), yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\int_0^\pi\int_0^\pi\int_0^\pi
 (4290k+367)X(p(\beta,\gamma),\alpha)^k
 \,d\alpha\,d\gamma\,d\beta\\
&\quad=\pi^3\frac{4290k+367}{3136^k}{2k\choose k}
 T_k(14,1)T_k(17,16). \tag{45}
\end{aligned}
\]

On the other hand, (42) and (1) imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^\pi\int_0^\pi\int_0^\pi
 f(p(\beta,\gamma),\alpha)
 \,d\alpha\,d\gamma\,d\beta
&=\pi\int_0^\pi\int_0^\pi F(\beta,\gamma)\,d\gamma\,d\beta\\
&=5390\pi^2. \tag{46}
\end{aligned}
\]
By (37), dominated convergence, and (45), the left side of (46) is
\[
 \pi^3\sum_{k=0}^\infty
 \frac{4290k+367}{3136^k}{2k\choose k}
 T_k(14,1)T_k(17,16).
\]
Therefore
\[
 \pi^3\sum_{k=0}^\infty
 \frac{4290k+367}{3136^k}{2k\choose k}
 T_k(14,1)T_k(17,16)=5390\pi^2.
\]
Since \(\pi\ne0\), division by \(\pi^3\) proves
\[
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \sum_{k=0}^\infty
 \frac{4290k+367}{3136^k}{2k\choose k}
 T_k(14,1)T_k(17,16)=\frac{5390}{\pi}}.
\]
